CHAIR ( Senator Marielle Smith ): I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 additional estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present, and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today. The committee has fixed Thursday 9 April 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with Corporate and Enabling Services in the education portfolio.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I welcome now Senator the Hon. Dr Jess Walsh, Minister for Early Childhood Education and the Minister for Youth, who is representing the Minister for Education. Minister, do you have an opening statement?

Senator Walsh: Good morning, Chair. No, I don't.

CHAIR: I now also welcome Mr Tony Cook PSM, Secretary of the Department of Education. I understand, Mr Cook, you do have an opening statement.

Mr Cook : That's right. Thank you very much. On behalf of the Department of Education, I begin by acknowledging the profound loss of life resulting from the Bondi Beach terrorist attack on 14 December 2025. Our thoughts remain with the 15 people who lost their lives, those who were injured and all who were affected by this devastating event. I extend my sincere condolences to the families and friends of those who died and to everyone who responded with such courage and compassion in the immediate aftermath of the attack. I also wish to acknowledge the deep and enduring impact this attack has had on the Australian Jewish community, who were the intended targets. As has been clearly stated across the parliament, there is no place in Australia for antisemitism, racial hatred or intolerance of any kind.

While the whole-of-government response to antisemitism extends beyond education alone, Australia's education system has a particularly important role to play. Our schools and universities are central to shaping understanding, fostering respect and equipping learners with the knowledge and values needed to understand and reject antisemitism and strengthen social cohesion. Addressing antisemitism across the education system is therefore a clear priority, and my department is fully committed to supporting this work.

As announced by the Prime Minister on 18 December 2025, Mr David Gonski AC has been appointed to lead a national antisemitism education taskforce. The taskforce has been tasked with supporting Australia's education system to prevent, address and respond to antisemitism. Mr Gonski brings to this role a longstanding commitment to education, inclusion and community cohesion. The taskforce, which includes Ms Jillian Segal AO, the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, has already met twice and will continue to meet on a monthly basis. Its initial focus is on four key streams of work: a targeted review of the Australian curriculum, after endorsement by education ministers in February; teacher training and professional development; strengthening the powers of TEQSA, the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency; and the development of a university report card, an initiative of the special envoy's plan to combat antisemitism, to assess how universities are responding to antisemitism. My department is supporting the taskforce in progressing the education measures announced as part of the government's response, including by providing advice on any additional actions that may be required.

Thanks, Chair. We look forward to assisting the committee with questions today. I've got that statement, which I will now table.

CHAIR: Thank you, Mr Cook. If we can get that distributed, that would be great. I am handing the call to Senator Kovacic. We're beginning with questions in relation to Corporate and Enabling Services.

Senator KOVACIC: Good morning, everyone. I'd like to start by asking some questions about the portfolio additional estimates statement. It notes a $358.7 million measure for education reprioritisation. Can you confirm that means that the overall funding profile for the department as a result of the MYEFO is a cut of $86.4 million over the forward estimates? That is my understanding—if I could just have a confirmation of that. I'm happy to repeat if needed.

Mr Boyd : The reprioritisation actually comes from two things; it's less a reduction. One of them is saves. There's $285.6 million over four years from 2025-26.

Senator KOVACIC: In saves?

Mr Boyd : Sorry—through additional integrity activities in relation to strengthening the childcare subsidy program.

Senator KOVACIC: Right.

Mr Boyd : It's actually work that's underway, including through the implementation of the new regulatory powers in relation to that program. The other component of the amount you mentioned is $73.1 million over three years, from 2025-26, which is the redirection of unallocated funds in relation to the Australia's Economic Accelerator program.

Senator KOVACIC: Alright. So it's a movement of the funds. Is it a reduction? Is there actually a reduction of that $86.4 million over the forward estimates or just a redistribution?

Mr Boyd : A redistribution—essentially those funds have been used to fund the measures within pays.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you.

Mr Cook : The first measure—I'll just make sure I'm right—is actually recovering money from the childcare sector where there's been inappropriate use of that money, as part of our integrity measure. Childcare services might have claimed for particular government funding; they might not have been entitled to that, because the number of children in that service may not be accurate. So part of what we're doing is actually bringing back money into the budget as a result of the activity of the department.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. So we've got the $285-odd million through integrity measures to the childcare subsidy.

Mr Cook : That's right.

Senator KOVACIC: And $73.1 million from the accelerator program. None of that has been reinvested into a research capacity, though, has it?

Mr Cook : I think, in terms of research, the numbers will be in the PAES as well in terms of the additional research funding that goes on. I'm just trying to find outcome 2.

Senator KOVACIC: What I'm trying to actually understand is whether that actually is an overall cut of $286 million to child care and what that actually looks like in practice. I'm just trying to work out if it's actually a reduction there. There's no material increase anywhere else.

Mr Cook : It's certainly not to cut child care. The childcare expenditure is going up significantly every year. It's a recouping of money that shouldn't actually have gone to services, because of how they've claimed that money. It's an integrity compliance measure.

Senator KOVACIC: So it was an overpayment?

Mr Cook : It was an overpayment based on the data that they had provided.

Senator KOVACIC: Right.

Mr Cook : When we undertook various exercises to check the data, we identified that they incorrectly claimed that money. So we have a compliance activity. I think there was a little bit of chat at ASQA last night that talked about the Fraud Fusion Taskforce. It's the activity that's part of that Fraud Fusion Taskforce. We're across government. We're finding providers that may be inaccurately claiming money and we're claiming that back or getting that back. And that's what that's about.

Senator KOVACIC: I have a document to table, document zero, if we could do that. And, once everyone's had an opportunity to look at that, I just want to ask about the measure under the permanent migration program 2025-26 planning levels, which includes significant variations to outcome 1. I'm just trying to understand the reallocation of the funds here.

Mr Cook : I'll turn to my experts to help me, but we've had this question before. As a result of decisions that are made in relation to migration, there are impacts on the number of kids that are going to child care or schools. And, if there are fewer people coming in or fewer people with families, then this is simply a reconciliation of that.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay, so basically you're saying if you've allocated X as a forward estimate and then you've had, let's say, 15 per cent lower uptake than required, basically, you haven't utilised those funds. So it's not actually a cut; it's actually just a reduction in the amount of money that you budgeted for.

Mr Cook : That you projected would be in the school system or the childcare system—this happens every single year. There's nothing unusual about this. I think it actually happens every budget cycle as well. It's just the updated, anticipated number in relation to migration.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay, so there's no reallocation, for example, of programs from schools being reallocated?

Mr Cook : No. This is not a program that we run. It's simply a reflection of, in terms of the totality of investment around child care and schools, updated parameters. That flows through to many departments. We're one of those departments where migrants might come in with young children and kids who are going to schools or universities too, probably.

Senator KOVACIC: So there's no impact to families, public schools or private schools—none at all? It's just expenditure that hasn't been utilised; it's been reallocated elsewhere.

Mr Cook : It's updated parameters.

Senator KOVACIC: Provisioning that hasn't been used and has been allocated elsewhere—okay. MYEFO also rolled over almost $10 million from the Community Child Care Fund and allocated it to current and future year. What were the circumstances or delays that made that rollover necessary?

Mr Boyd : Broadly, it was due to delays, such as where decisions have been taken in relation to payments under the program, particularly the delays related to things like adverse weather events, floods, drought and those kinds of things, as well as being able to get some of the services in very remote type areas. So the delays are predominantly of that kind of nature.

Senator KOVACIC: In terms of total expenditure on outcome 1, it appears that there is a cost blowout of some $544 million between the 2025-26 budget and the revised estimates, and that's from page 26 in PBS and page 32 in PAES. Is that correct? Are those figures accurate?

Mr Boyd : I don't have my PBS with me, but I would note that outcome 1 has a number of special appropriation funded programs. By their nature, they're demand driven. So the funding flows depending on the level of demand.

Senator KOVACIC: Gotcha.

Mr Boyd : So, if the level of demand goes up, then the expected outlay in relation to that program would go up and the funding increases accordingly.

Senator KOVACIC: Could you give me an example of the type of program where that might occur?

Mr Cook : Schools are a classic example—as a result of increased numbers of students with disability, or as a result of more students going to the non-government sector versus the government sector. The other example would be child care. As a result of more families taking up child care, the parameters change every budget cycle. And this is what's happened again.

Senator KOVACIC: The $500 million is a large figure. I note that it's demand driven, but that is a lot. Is there anything significant that caused that increase or blowout or whatever somebody would want to call it?

Mr Boyd : Without being able to step through the specific programs there, it's hard to say. Apart from that, we know there's a number of large demand driven programs there; it's hard to actually go to what the specifics of each of those are. Officers from the relevant outcome might be able to talk to their specific areas in there, so the schools people might be able to describe why there's a change, for example.

Senator KOVACIC: Are you able to provide the breakdown and perhaps a brief explanation on notice?

Mr Cook : I can probably help with some. I've got both documents in front of me now. In terms of non-government school support, in the PBS it talked about roughly $19.9 billion. In PAES, it talks about $20.5 billion. So you can see there's a big increase there around the non-government, and that would be a combination of both more families choosing non-government schools and also the increase in the number for disability in non-government schools as well. Again, it's not unusual. This happens every budget cycle, but that gives you an example of a relatively significant change in terms of our parameters model—what we had anticipated would be the take-up of both government and non-government schools.

Senator KOVACIC: I don't need the specific numbers for this, unless you have them, but what other segments would be in there? Obviously, non-government is one of those. What else would be in there as a large shift? I think you said $19 million.

Mr Cook : Was it my billion or your million you were talking about? I talked about $19 billion.

Senator KOVACIC: I'm trying to get an understanding of where the variance of the $544 million came from.

Mr Cook : Okay. Mr Markovic can help, because I think the detailed explanation is actually in MYEFO.

Mr Markovic : I think you're asking for what the significant contributions are.

Senator KOVACIC: Correct, yes.

Mr Markovic : Pages 67 and 68 of MYEFO list those. The most significant for our portfolio in 2025-26 is, as the secretary has mentioned, payments to non-government schools of $505 million in 2025-26. There is also another item for our portfolio listed, which is a minor reduction in the childcare subsidy program of $149 million. There will be some other non-material ones, but the material items to your earlier question to the CFO are listed, on pages 67 and 68 of MYEFO.

Senator KOVACIC: In terms of expenditure on outcome 2, could you confirm for me that, in the 2025 budget, there was $8.63 billion allocated to core Commonwealth funding for teaching and learning in higher education, but in MYEFO that has been reduced to $8.27 billion? That's a drop of $356 million in core Commonwealth funding for higher education. Is that accurate? Have I understood that correctly?

Mr Cook : The figures I've got in front of me are $8.6 billion, which I think is the figure you gave me—

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, $8.63 billion. Correct.

Mr Cook : And for PAES I've got $8.27 billion.

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, so it is a drop of $356 million?

Mr Cook : And this will be projection in terms of student numbers and what that looks like going forward, as it would normally be.

Senator KOVACIC: So, to clarify, that's not a drop in funding; that's a drop in the amount of money that has been required to be spent based on the number of students that have taken it up.

Mr Cook : Yes. That's my understanding. I think we'd have a total amount. I'll see if someone might be able to help me. Do we have a total amount for outcome 2? Do we have that at all, in terms of all funding we give outcome 2?

Mr Boyd : Yes—$27.6 billion for outcome 2 is the current revised estimate.

Mr Cook : And what was it at budget?

Mr Boyd : At budget, it was $15.6 billion.

Mr Cook : So there's a $10 billion increase. Now, obviously, part of that's about HELP debt, but there's been a significant increase in outcome 2 between budget and PAES as well.

Senator KOVACIC: Alright. So you're basically saying that there's no impact—that there is no actual cut there?

Mr Cook : We can go into a bit more detail on higher education if you want to go into the detail around some of these things—

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, please.

Mr Cook : but, in terms of managed growth and needs based funding, I think it would be good for that level of detail in the higher education section, if you're okay with that?

Senator KOVACIC: Yes, absolutely.

Mr Cook : Thank you—because my officers are well prepared for those questions later on.

Senator KOVACIC: I'm just having a think about the core Commonwealth funding for teaching and higher learning in higher education. Again, you're talking about it being demand driven and that there's actually no cut. Can you take me through that again and explain how the funding has not been reduced. You're saying it's demand driven in reverse. Does that reduce the overall pool in the future, or does that then increase?

Mr Cook : Not necessarily. As you'd be aware, the minister has indicated there are 9,500 additional Commonwealth supported places this calendar year, and up to 16,000 additional Commonwealth supported places next year. Part of this was through the Universities Accord reforms and the work of the Australian Tertiary Education Commission. Again, they'll be here later for higher education if you want to go into detail. There were decisions made that, where universities had not reached their MGBA, their maximum grant allocation, they would not receive indexation—because, in fact, they didn't have the students enrolled and they were receiving more money than that for the number of students they have enrolled. So they'll get the same this year as they got last year, but indexation won't be applied. There are some changes in terms of methodology.

Again, I'm very happy to go into that level of detail, because we've got to add needs based funding, and then we've got to add managed growth. Higher education is probably a little bit easier—if that's okay with you, Senator—to ask for the detail of what that looks like, because the people that actually look after the funding of universities will be here for that item.

Senator KOVACIC: Yes. So, just to confirm, so you don't call the reduction in spending of that $356 million a cut, effectively, on the basis that it's a demand driven thing. So you're not cutting it. They haven't taken it up. So you haven't cut it because there's no demand for it effectively, so you don't need to spend it.

Mr Cook : That's right. No university will get less than they received last year on the basis of their student numbers. A number of universities will get more, and there's an allocation of the 9,500 additional Commonwealth supported places. But there's a guarantee that a university will not get less funding than what they got last year, so effectively there's no cut.

Senator KOVACIC: Yes. So, effectively, the spending on the core Commonwealth funding for teaching and learning in higher education, even though it's dropped by $356 million, is because there is no demand.

Mr Cook : Effectively—because, again, the projections were based on particular parameters in terms of what we thought the domestic load would be. That domestic load has been different to what was anticipated. That's right.

Senator KOVACIC: The domestic load has been $356 million less?

Mr Cook : Effectively, because, as a result of—

Senator KOVACIC: What does 'effectively' mean—just so I understand?

Mr Cook : Effectively, because some universities haven't enrolled the number of students that we had anticipated, they're not getting the increase that was factored into the parameters. They will get the same amount of money they got last year, so there's no cut to those universities, but they won't get an anticipated increase that they would have got if we anticipated that they enrolled more students than they actually have.

Senator KOVACIC: So that projection—or let's just call it that $350 million that was anticipated that would be utilised in resourcing that wasn't. How was that number derived to begin with? How did we end up $356 million lower in demand than we had budgeted for?

Mr Cook : It's the same sort of question that you could have for child care and schools. For any demand driven program, we have parameter models where we effectively put into the model, 'This is what we expect the increase would be in terms of student demand,' whether in child care, schools or higher education. That goes into the model. It goes over the forward estimates. Those parameters are changed every budget update to reflect any latest data that we've got.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. So basically, based on the modelling, there was an estimate of the number of children that would go through to university, and that didn't eventuate. That was $350-odd million less than expected.

Mr Cook : They might have gone to VET; they might have chosen to go into the workforce—whatever the case may be. So that's effectively correct.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. Is that an unusual variance? Is that in the standard range that you would normally have?

Mr Cook : I don't think it's unusual. No-one's raised it with me as being unusual. My costing boffins tell me it's not. Again, we try and just get as much up-to-date information as we can about behaviours.

Senator KOVACIC: That could be cyclical variances or something else.

Mr Cook : Exactly.

Senator KOVACIC: Do you have any insights on what, apart from obviously cyclical elements, might be drivers of changes in demand in different years or in different periods?

Mr Cook : On universities?

Senator KOVACIC: Yes.

Mr Cook : It could be the job market. If the job market is quite buoyant, we often find that students take a gap year; they might go straight into the job market. Where we find the employment market is a bit challenging, we often find students coming to university at a greater rate than we might have anticipated. So those sorts of things are the main factors in relation to it as well.

Senator KOVACIC: I have a quick question on average staffing levels. The average staffing levels grew from 1,633 last year to 1,700 this year, according to the portfolio additional estimates statement. The average staffing level in October 2022 was 1,292. Just on a rough cut, that's about a 30 per cent growth of staff in the department in just over three years. Can you give me some insights on that and the requirements around that and the sustainability of that as well?

Mr Cook : Mr Markovic has a step-by-step breakdown on that.

Senator KOVACIC: That would be great. Thank you.

Mr Markovic : I can talk through each of the changes in ASL. It's about a page and a half worth, or would you like me to pick out perhaps some of the major items?

Senator KOVACIC: If you could pick out some of the major items, talk to them and perhaps table the document, that would be great.

Mr Markovic : Probably the major items have been an investment in childcare integrity measures, which the secretary spoke to earlier. That has been a significant focus across the department, and there are a few different measures over the four budget updates that contribute to that. There are a couple of things that have happened and then reversed out of the process, but that's a significant one. The department has received additional resourcing to support the implementation of the ECEC wage subsidy. That was a grant program, and we do have some additional resourcing for that. I'm just trying to pick out—there's a long list. I'm trying to find things over 20 as a parameter. There is child safety. In the most recent budget update, so between the 1,633 that you mentioned and the 1,700, 99 per cent of that resourcing was for child safety work that our minister announced last year, and other than that there's one ASL that isn't that. So they're the key areas, but certainly we have an itemisation of all the ons and offs that we can provide to you on notice.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. Looking at that 30 per cent growth in that period of three years, is that something that is expected to stabilise at this point? Is that something that's because we've required that additional safety in the childcare integrity measures and the child safety, particularly with what we've seen occurring in childcare centres? Is that something that we believe we have covered now or do you think there will need to be a further investment in resourcing, particularly if we move to a universal childcare model?

Mr Cook : Sure. They are really questions for government to make decisions out of every budget.

Senator KOVACIC: Have you been asked to do any modelling on that?

Mr Cook : Modelling on?

Senator KOVACIC: No. I want to get an understanding of who triggered the first briefing for 19 June and then on what date the first offer or request for the briefing was made. Was Minister Clare also briefed on 19 June? I'm happy to take that on notice. That is the context of what I'm trying to understand.

Senator Walsh: The department can correct me. In general, I became aware that a briefing is required via the department. The department may have further information about that.

Mr Cook : It really depends on the individual cases, Senator. Sometimes the briefings are offered by the AFP to ministers. In this case, I'm sorry, but I don't know. I think we will take it on notice so that we can provide that information to you.

Senator KOVACIC: Prior to 1 July 2025, were any other ministers made aware of the cases that were made public on 1 July? I'm trying to get an idea of the timeline and where things fit. It appears that the government and the minister were aware at least in general terms about the Joshua Brown allegations prior to 1 July, which is when they were publicly released.

Mr Cook : In general terms, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: We infer that because of the evidence about not being briefed on the centres and the discussions with the Victorian minister. We know that happened before the Education Ministers Meeting, which was on 27 June; it was maybe a week before. We know that there was a briefing from the AFP on 19 June, though we don't know the contents of that meeting. I'm not asking you to provide them. I am trying to understand if that is a correct timeline.

Mr Cook : I think that is accurate. That is on the basis that, as you know, all that is under the timing of the suppression order as well.

Senator KOVACIC: Yes. I note—

Mr Cook : So the detail of that—

Senator KOVACIC: there was a suppression order, yes. There is no question about that. I just want to understand it.

Mr Cook : I believe you are accurate.

Senator KOVACIC: It looks like there was probably around a 12-day period—I'm happy to be corrected—that the government had this information before it became public. I want to understand what happened during that time. Was it an opportunity to generate policy options to prepare for a response and develop a stakeholder communication plan to engage with families? What were the actions that came once that information came to light, noting the necessity of protecting the fact that there was a suppression order?

Mr Cook : My understanding is that, as a result of the general knowledge ministers were aware of, there was actually a special early childhood ministers only meeting called. The focus of that meeting was on child safety.

Senator KOVACIC: When was that?

Mr Cook : I should know. We'll have to find the date.

Senator Walsh: My recollection—Ms Crane may need to assist on notice—is that there were two EMMs on child safety. One was a standard meeting, but child safety was the top priority in the early education portfolio. There was then a standalone child safety meeting.

Mr Cook : So 27 June is when the meeting was held where it was agreed there would be a special purpose early childhood meeting. That special purpose early childhood meeting happened on 22 August. At the 27 June meeting, there was significant discussion of child safety, reflecting an understanding of some of the developments that were happening in the Victorian case.

Senator KOVACIC: I'm trying to work out what period of time the department and the government had between becoming aware and the suppression order being lifted. At what point in that time did most families become aware? There is a concern by families who feel that maybe they didn't find out soon enough that there was a period of time or a lag in time before they found out. Perhaps government officials knew before they knew. What was occurring during that time? Are we able to go back to that point? What was the government and the department doing between 19 and 27 June and 1 July, when different levels of awareness as to the allegations against Joshua Brown became prevalent?

Ms Crane : Perhaps I can answer that from two angles. I will address the EMM on 27 June first because there were substantive items on there around child safety. You might recall that ACEQA had done a child safety review. Discussion around the recommendations from that review that came from another case was a significant part of that meeting and decisions by ministers at that meeting. In terms of the department's involvement—I think we answered some of this in a previous QON—we became aware of the matter on 20 June. That is not the details of the matter or who it was. As part of that, we were asked to provide data, which we would do as part of investigations. The data we provided would have formed what the Victorian officials then used to determine which families needed to be contacted or where this individual worked. From our perspective, our role with Victoria is supporting them or any other official that is undertaking the investigation. That is the extent of that with that matter. The rest of the work that the department will have been doing was responding to the other recommendations and the child safety actions that had come out of ACEQA's review.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. I will finish up with this and maybe one more question. Were any other departments informed during that period before the suppression order was lifted, such as PM&C or Finance? Do we know?

Ms Crane : We don't have this ability. We didn't advise any other departments.

Senator KOVACIC: You don't know. Minister, do you know?

Senator Walsh: Sorry, could you repeat the question?

Senator KOVACIC: Do you know whether any other departments were informed before the suppression order was lifted—say, PM&C or Finance?

Senator Walsh: No. I think I need to reiterate to you that both Minister Clare and I, as previously said, were briefed in very general terms—not given the name or nature and extent of the offences—because of the suppression order.

Senator KOVACIC: So did you find out all of those details when the suppression order was lifted?

Senator Walsh: That's correct.

Senator KOVACIC: So you had no knowledge of all the details before the suppression order was lifted?

Senator Walsh: That's correct, yes.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you.

Senator DOLEGA: I have questions about childcare affordability access and flexibility. I would like to ask some questions about the latest childcare subsidy data. In particular, how much has the average family saved because of cheaper child care? How much is that per year?

Mr Reed : The average family, based on average income and average fees in the childcare system, has saved approximately $3½ thousand a year, or over the first three years of implementation about $11,400 through the cheaper childcare changes.

Senator DOLEGA: That is fantastic. While we're talking about this, can I ask you for information about the impact of the fee constraint condition for the worker retention payment. For example, is there a difference in fee growth between services that have applied for the wage funding and those that haven't? Could you talk me through it.

Mr Reed : Sure. One of the conditions of the worker retention payment is that there is a fee constraint on services that apply. The fee constraint was 4.4 per cent for the first year and then 4.2 per cent currently. Our administrative data shows that services that have signed up and have an active worker retention payment grant have increased their fees on average 3.5 per cent in the first year of the program compared to 7.1 per cent for those that are not signed up for the WA. So it got about half the growth in fees compared to those not in the program.

Senator DOLEGA: Thanks, Mr Reed. As you would be aware, on 5 January, Labor's three-day guarantee took effect. It guarantees eligibility for 72 hours of childcare subsidy per fortnight, or three days per week, for all children who need it. Can you give me some examples of how the three-day guarantee can help families with the cost of child care?

Mr Reed : Sure. I will call Ms Astill-Torchia to the table, who might have a bit more information. Essentially, the three-day guarantee provides more subsidised hours in care. So families that previously didn't have access to subsidised care or had access to a low level of subsidised care can now access 72 hours a fortnight, or essentially three days of care a fortnight, regardless of their activity level. It gives that guarantee of places and subsidised hours. I can give you some cameos. I might refer to Ms Astill-Torchia to give some cameos on family outcomes.

Ms Astill-Torchia : The department has modelled a few cameos to map out the benefits for families as a result of this measure. As part of modelling who will benefit from 5 January, the department modelled that around 66,700 families would be better off come 5 January in the 2026-27 year. Of that group, families earning between $50,000 and $100,000 a year would be around $1,460 better off per year. That looks at the modelled cohort and the financial benefits that would come across different income bands. We've also looked at the maximum benefits for families who are now accessing the 72 hours of care. For example, a lower income family earning $90,000 with one child in care could save up to $230 a week on child care, which is pretty significant.

Senator DOLEGA: Absolutely. Thank you for that data. Minister, I know that many families in my home state of Tasmania understand the importance of access to high-quality early childhood education and care. I note your recent commitment to build more early learning services in Tassie and that these new services are in addition to the Australian government funding a critical service, Lady Gowrie, in La Trobe. Can you tell me what this means for Tasmania?

Senator Walsh: We have been doing a lot to invest in quality early childhood education to support children and families across Tasmania. One part of that is actually through a big agreement that we signed with the Tasmanian government as part of our building early childhood education fund. We also signed an agreement with the ACT government. Just this week I was able to go and see the site of a new childcare centre that will be built as part of that fund here in Canberra. We know that in Tasmania there are a lot of children in a lot of areas who don't have the access that we would like to quality early childhood education. Indeed, some parts of Tasmania are underserved. Some of this was brought to our attention by someone who is very well known in these rooms, which is former senator Anne Urquhart, now the member for Braddon, who invited me down to the La Trobe region to learn about some of the challenges there. We heard there about a significant issue where there was going to be a closure of a service and a new centre opening several months later. There was going to be a six-month gap in the provision of services to families. That would have been really disruptive for not only the children but also the parents and their ability to have their children in quality early education and work. We were able to work with the member for Braddon and the Tasmanian Minister for Education Jo Palmer. The Commonwealth is providing Lady Gowrie, which is a great not-for-profit provider, with a grant under the community childcare fund of $334,000. It's a great outcome for that community in La Trobe to have a quality not-for-profit provider delivering early learning. That Lady Gowrie service is opening an interim service soon.

In relation to the agreement with Tasmania, as part of the Building Early Education Fund, we will deliver six not-for-profit early learning services across Tasmania. That is a $25.5 million investment through that billion-dollar Building Early Education Fund. The Tasmanian government is also providing an additional $5 million as well. The projects will be at Westbury Primary, Rosetta Primary, St Mary's District School, Bruny Island District School, Bothwell District High School and Huonville Primary School. It's really great that these services will be co-located at schools. It is good for children to help them get ready for school to see the big school that is there. Early childhood education is great for getting children ready for school. It is even better when it's co-located with the school. It is great for families as well to help them deal with the double drop-off.

This is a big investment in children in Tasmania. We know that quality early childhood education is good for children. It's good for parents. This is going to be great for our Tasmanian communities as well.

Senator DOLEGA: As La Trobe is my home town as well, I drive past and see the progress on Lady Gowrie. I know that the community is going to be so relieved to have that urgent support so there's no gap and people can stay in work. Thank you, Minister. If I still have some time, I have some questions for the department about Closing the Gap. Can you give me an update on the number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children who are attending CCS approved care? Can you tell me how that compares with previous years?

Ms Winslow : In the latest available childcare subsidy data in September 2025, we did have 68,150 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in receipt of the childcare subsidy. That was a 4.73 increase on the previous year's data.

Senator DOLEGA: Thank you, Ms Winslow. The ANAO's audit report Closing the gap in early childhood and schooling highlights some concerns in relation to the preschool reform agenda and its alignment to the national agreement on Closing the Gap. Can you talk me through the issue and what the department is doing to resolve the matter?

Ms Winslow : With respect to the ANAO findings, the reference is made to the negotiations of the Preschool Reform Agreement. They were with respect to negotiations several years ago. There is work underway currently in the preschool reform space to actively engage our relevant First Nation peaks and partners, including SNAICC—National Voice for our Children and the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Education Corporation. We certainly have been working actively and in partnership on the current negotiations under the PRA. I'm not sure if Mr Reed wants to add to that.

Mr Reed : That's right. I guess we considered lessons learned from the previous consultation process with the previous PRA process. I guess we are picking up best practices through things such as the school agreement. For the extension of the PRA, we engaged really constructively and closely with our First Nation peak organisations. We are doing that now with the ongoing preschool reform governance arrangements as well. We have membership of First Nations peaks on those governance bodies.

Senator DOLEGA: I want to focus on that work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in partnership with governments to derive community-led early childhood care and development. Can you give us an update on the work for early childhood care and development policy partnerships?

Ms Winslow : I'm certainly happy to answer that question. We have now been running in partnership with SNAICC the early childhood care and development policy partnership. It is a joint initiative with all governments and our First Nations peaks that work in the early childhood space. We were pleased by the findings in that ANAO report that you mentioned around the strong partnership that mechanism has been able to establish and demonstrate. In the MYEFO process at the end of 2024-25, we did have a second term of funding allocated to that policy partnership. I think in recognition of the maturity of the partnership, we have been able over time to demonstrate how it is supporting better outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. It was responsible for commissioning research to further build the evidence base around effective models of support for First Nations children and the optimal hours of care for First Nations children with respect to early childhood education and care. The research commissioned by the partnership was provided to the Productivity Commission inquiry into early childhood education and care. In part along with other evidence considered by the inquiry, it did inform key recent changes that were talked about earlier in this session, including the increase in subsidised hours of care for First Nations children under the changes that came in this year. So it has been able to generate evidence and inform policy. It is working across all relevant portfolios in the early childhood space, including to address issues such as the increasing engagement of children in not only health but also social services. So it is a broad, whole-of-government initiative.

Senator DOLEGA: I do look forward to hearing about this each estimates, so I look forward to talking to you again soon.

Senator PAYMAN: I would like to ask if the committee is okay with me tabling an email?

CHAIR: You can distribute that one. The committee will need to make a later decision on tabling.

Senator PAYMAN: No worries. On 17 April 2025, during the 2025 election campaign, Labor candidate for Durack in WA Karen Wheatland announced that a re-elected Albanese Labor government will invest up to $5 million towards building a new childcare centre in Mukinbudin. What work has been done to honour this commitment since the election? Perhaps the minister can take it.

Senator Walsh: Yes, that is a commitment. It's part of our building early childhood education fund that is building services in underserved areas, including in Western Australia. We are working with the Western Australian government on those commitments. Mr Smyth may provide further details.

Mr Smyth : Yes, we have been actively engaged with the Western Australian government in relation to that election commitment as well as the two other election commitments made in Western Australia. We are yet to reach a final agreement with the Western Australian government. I've also had discussions with the local council in Mukinbudin as well in relation to the need for services in that area. Those discussions are ongoing. The commitment remains.

Senator PAYMAN: So we can say that you have received input or action from the shire of Mukinbudin?

Mr Smyth : I've had some discussions with them around the commitment, yes.

Senator PAYMAN: Can you tell me when those discussions took place? The CEO wrote to us in September 2025 expressing that there hasn't really been any update. For a Western Australian senator to bring these questions forward to an estimates hearing to get an update for a local shire, it doesn't give us confidence that there has been work behind the scenes. That is why these questions are being brought to you.

Mr Smyth : I understand. I will take on notice the exact date that I met with the shire. It would have been around, from memory, that September-October period that I actually met with them and had a discussion.

Senator PAYMAN: Minister, have you received any correspondence from the shire of Mukinbudin on this issue?

Senator Walsh: I would not want to provide you with incorrect information, so I will take that on notice.

Senator PAYMAN: Yes. Please do. Thank you. Is there a rough timeline you can provide to the people of Mukinbudin to see when this commitment will be honoured?

Mr Smyth : I wouldn't like to pre-empt the negotiations that are going on and the reaching of an agreement at this point in time. I think I have a meeting with Western Australian officials lined up for next week as well.

Senator PAYMAN: You said that there are a few commitments. Can you outline other areas in Western Australia where a commitment was made aside from the shire of Mukinbudin?

Mr Smyth : There were two. There is Maarakool and Mundaring as well as Mukinbudin. It seems to be something with the 'M's I think in Western Australia.

Senator PAYMAN: We often feel very neglected in WA. Given the billion-dollar Building Early Education Fund—there hasn't been much progress; it is sitting idle—when is the government planning to start actually getting the ball rolling around childcare deserts?

Mr Smyth : I would not, I suppose, classify it by saying that we haven't made any progress and it's sitting idle. Substantial amounts of work have been undertaken over the last six to seven months in relation to the Building Early Education Fund. We've undertaken two market soundings for small providers and large providers. We've entered into three federation funding agreements with South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT. We have ongoing negotiations with other jurisdictions around those federation funding agreements. We are also negotiating the election commitments made by the government and incorporating them into those federation funding agreements. On Monday this week, we opened our large provider grant round. We will shortly, subject to the minister's agreement on timing, open a small provider grant round as well. I would say that substantial progress has been made. In addition to the investment dialogue for Australia's children, where we've reached agreement on how we will go about agreeing to particular projects, we are co-investing funding for integrated hub centres. They are based around the ECECs as well. So quite a substantial amount of work has been undertaken.

Senator PAYMAN: Yet we still don't have a timeline, even generally. Let's not specifically talk about WA. Generally, is there a timeline for when the funding that has been committed will actually roll out and we'll see the funding reaching the very childcare deserts we have?

Mr Smyth : The Treasury will make a number of payments in relation to federation funding agreements next month. We will also see contracting for services once we've undertaken appropriate assessments of grant applications that we receive through the small and large provider rounds. Funding will start to immediately flow out of them as well. As you would appreciate, construction projects take time. They have to have the correct approvals in place. People have to contract particular construction firms et cetera. So it doesn't happen in an instant. We want to take a methodical and well-chartered approach to the way we undertake this. It's a substantial amount of taxpayers' money and we want to administer it in an appropriate way.

Senator PAYMAN: Absolutely. I'm not asking it to be rushed. Everyone is waiting to see progress.

Mr Smyth : I understand that.

Senator PAYMAN: I appreciate you guys taking it on notice to get back to me about the shire of Mukinbudin.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Thank you for joining us today. I will start off with one of my favourite questions that I ask repeatedly. I am keen to know if anything has changed since December on whether the department has prepared any advice, modelling or costings to the government on the Productivity Commission recommendation of an early childhood education and care commission?

Ms Crane : No, we have not done any modelling.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: This was a key consideration and recommendation of the Productivity Commission report. We have heard in evidence to our quality and early learning inquiry that this has been recommended by multiple stakeholders. I am wondering why the department hasn't taken on board consideration of that proposal.

Ms Crane : Ultimately, that is a decision for government. In terms of what the Productivity Commission has recommended, there are a number of other elements in there. Government has taken steps on a wide range of them, some of which we have spoken about at the table today and in past sessions.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Minister, do you have any explanation as to why you haven't requested that advice, or is it something that you are considering requesting of the department?

Senator Walsh: So in relation to the Productivity Commission review, as Ms Crane said, we're implementing the findings and recommendations of that review in a number of ways. One of the main focuses of the review was on the workforce. Another was on affordability. Another was on access. So in relation to the workforce, obviously the 15 per cent pay rise is paying dividends in stabilising the workforce. In relation to affordability, we've done a number of things, including our cheaper childcare reforms, which will save the average family $3½ thousand in fees this year on what they would otherwise have paid. We are capping the fee growth of services at 3½ per cent and introducing the three-day guarantee, which is—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I'm aware of the others. I'm specifically asking about the commission.

Senator Walsh: In terms of the Building Early Education Fund, we are expanding access to services in areas that are underserved. We are implementing the Productivity Commission recommendations in the work that we are doing. You are referring to a recommendation in relation to an early childhood education commission. I have answered this question to you before in various settings. Our focus is on safety. At the moment, our focus is on the workforce. Our focus is on affordability. Our focus is on access. We're taking action on all of those things. We have always said, and continue to say today, that a commission could be part of future reforms.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: It does seem that the establishment of the commission could assist with each of those different areas that you've identified.

Senator Walsh: Well, we're already doing them.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have questions about the efficacy of some of those and the ongoing nature of them coming up in my next round of questions. I'm encouraged to hear that it still hasn't been ruled out. I will keep asking until we get some confirmation of progress on that. I have some questions next up about the In Home Care program. In-home care providers originated from the greater flexibility and choice in childcare elements of the Australian government's Stronger Families and Communities Strategy back in 2000. As you would be aware, these providers provide care to children who can't attend centre based ECEC, such as the children of shift workers, children in rural areas as well as children with families with complex and significant needs. Minister, to start off, does the Labor government still consider In Home Care as an important pillar of choice for early childhood education and care in Australia?

Senator Walsh: We continue to provide support to that program. In-home care services provide a flexible form of early childhood education, taking place in the family home. It is targeted to assisting parents who are unable to access other approved care types. We continue to support that program.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have received a significant volume of correspondence in recent weeks from in-home care providers who are currently preparing the families they serve for significantly increased out-of-pocket costs from March due to the long overdue gender undervaluation reforms. Has the department done any modelling or do you know how much this might cost on average a family accessing in-home care services given the current hourly In Home Care rate?

Mr Reed : I would have to take on notice whether we have done modelling on the impact of the Fair Work Commission wage increase. Is that what you mean? I will have to take on notice whether we've done any modelling. We've definitely considered the impacts of the Fair Work Commission work on the sector and the different subcare types in the sector. As was previously said, we are considering the impacts. The government has said it is considering if and how to extend the worker retention payment to those subsectors, but no decision has been made in relation to that.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: It would be good if you could provide on notice any modelling that you have. That would be appreciated. Providers have told us that easily upward of $1,000 per week will be passed on to families from March. Minister, do you think that's a reasonable sum of money for families to be expected to find to keep this critical service?

Senator Walsh: I haven't seen that data. In relation to the worker retention payment, obviously, this is a $3.6 billion commitment. It is focused on the 15 per cent pay rise. The gender undervaluation payment decision, as you know, came out because the government put gender equality as a goal of the Fair Work Act. We continue to work through the gender undervaluation decision. In relation to the in-home care workforce, I think Mr Reed has taken that on notice. I understand that there is work underway to figure out how to assist that sector to best support the workforce in relation to pay rises. Maybe Ms Crane has better detail on that. I understand that some work is underway.

Ms Crane : Mr Reed has said that we will provide what we can on notice. We will do that. I will unpack one part that the minister and Mr Reed said. There are different employment arrangements under In Home Care. Of course, that has been partly why we've needed to go and do more work on this. In terms of the considerations of the government, we need to think about the differences in what that looks like.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: These providers did notify me that they had provided this data to the minister, so I will ask them to perhaps resend it in relation to that $1,000 per week. It was my understanding that in-home care providers aren't actually eligible for the worker retention payment currently. Is that correct?

Mr Reed : Not currently.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: They are not. That is probably less relevant. I suppose the consequence of passing this cost on to families is actually more gender inequality, particularly for women, who are being forced to decide whether they now need to stay at home instead of participate in the workforce. I think it is a very pressing issue for many families across the country. Can the department please tell me more about the urgent advice they are preparing? Did you say you are? Does this include potentially increasing the hourly cap for In Home Care?

Mr Reed : We are preparing advice for government on the impacts of the Fair Work Commission decision and how that can be best dealt with. In relation to the hourly rate caps, I think the important thing is that any changes to those kind of CCS settings are evidence informed. We are undertaking a service delivery price that will provide really good evidence on the cost of delivering care between the different sectors. I think the service delivery price will be a key piece of evidence that could inform future changes to any of the CCS settings. So the work we're doing currently is really how we can best support those sectors in relation to the Fair Work Commission decision to increase the award rate.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Do you think that will happen in time for March, when these pay increases are going to happen?

Mr Reed : Changes to the program? I think changes to the program would be unlikely by March because of the time it would take to implement changes to the program, such as to develop guidelines. So I couldn't put a timeframe on it. We are actively considering the impacts and providing advice to government for those in-home care and family daycare sectors. As Ms Crane pointed out, there are complexities to those sectors in how you could extend the payment in its current form primarily due to the employment model for a lot of those providers.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: So, in the meantime, we can assume that there is nothing going to be put in place to stop that cost being passed on in March? There is no stopgap that will be in place for these families that are concerned about this.

Mr Reed : Well, there are current settings that would subsidise costs in those sectors. The childcare subsidy primarily subsidises a significant cost for those sectors. But I couldn't put a timeframe on any changes to existing programs.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Out of interest, what is the current hourly cap that the IHC program is based on?

Mr Reed : I'll get that for you. I won't guess.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: It is $39. I'm keen to know what that sum is based on and how it has been derived.

Mr Reed : The initial rate was set at the time the childcare subsidy program was implemented. It has been indexed since then with CPI. I would have to take on notice the things that went into the initial setting of that hourly rate cap back in 2018 when the childcare subsidy system was introduced. All rate caps are indexed with CPI.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Could you take on notice whether it takes into consideration any of the overheads of IHC providers in addition?

Mr Reed : I can take that on notice.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Thank you. Minister, IHC providers have detailed evidence that the hourly rate of $39 is nowhere near enough to cover the costs of skilled and qualified educators. I think this is on top of a lot of evidence from the IHC review. The ACCC and the Productivity Commission work you've already got at your disposal. I'm interested to hear if you have any comments on why this hasn't been addressed and why, in February, these changes are going to come into place in March and these families are going to be faced with this funding gap and the potential need to return home to care to educate their kids when they're priced out of in-home care, essentially.

Senator Walsh: I refer you to the work of the department, Senator. The program continues to be supported by the government. There is work going on in the department around the program on wage issues and arrangements in the program. We continue to support the program, including through the childcare subsidy.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have to say that many of these families don't feel like they are being supported. They are telling us about the need to unenroll their children. They are drafting resignation letters. They're warning that educators' jobs might be lost. I'm not sure how much comfort that brings to these people. I urge the department and you, Minister, to prioritise a solution to this for those families who are feeling immense anxiety as March rapidly rolls around.

Senator KOVACIC: I want to go back to the questions I was asked before about the timelines in relation to the Joshua Brown allegations and briefings. I want to table documents 6 to 13, if that is possible. Minister, on around 20 June—there are some things on social media between 20 and 23 June, but I suggest it was on 20 June—you visited a childcare centre with Minister Clare in the Melbourne electorate of Maribyrnong. I would like to get an understanding of whether you were briefed by the department for this visit. Did that brief include whether this centre was an affected centre? Had you thought about whether it possibly was given the briefing you had received the day before? Did you ask the department to check either with its own data or with the Victorian government as to whether it was an affected centre?

Senator Walsh: I'll await their document. You will have to jog my memory. Ms Crane can assist.

Senator KOVACIC: Sure.

Ms Crane : We would provide for any visit information around the sorts of supports that the Australian government provides or compliance action that we've undertaken. We wouldn't have access to some of that, just in a broader sense, around what other things might be happening in a state or territory. In terms of even that time line you've talked about, at that stage, the phone call that I took was on 20 June. We hadn't received the data request at that stage to even know that there were any services picked up, nor would we have known the nature of what the actual incidents were around that.

Senator KOVACIC: I want to clarify again. The department found out on 1 July when the suppression order was lifted all of the detail in the same time that the minister did. Is that correct?
