Mr Reed : Discrepancy? Sorry, could you—

Senator KOVACIC: The increase, the variance. We've got a fee cap of 4.4 per cent or 4.2 per cent. The CPI data is saying it's 11.2 per cent. You indicated earlier that there are a number of factors. Are you aware of one of those factors involving any particular behaviour by operators? Are there operators who are increasing their prices?

Mr Reed : All operators will increase their fees regularly, usually on an annual basis. But we know that, compared to the long-term average, at an aggregate level, operators are increasing their fees less than they have been. That's, at least, partly due to the worker retention payment fee constraint policy. But not all services are in the worker retention payment. We know that those services who are not in the worker retention payment, which is just over 20 per cent of services, are increasing their fees at double the rate that services within the worker retention payment are. That would be having an impact on the aggregate level of childcare CPI increases. But, as I said, there are many factors. It does not measure the increase in fees. It measures the increase in out-of-pocket costs, and that could be for a variety of reasons, such as increased hours. It could be that there's a higher level of higher cost children in the system.

Senator KOVACIC: I want to ask you about increased hours. That was the rest of my question. Are you seeing centres increasing their hours? If a centre changes their hours from 10 hours a day to 11 or 12 hours a day, then a family is obliged to still have their child registered for that full day but they don't require the 12 hours, are they having to pay for that additional couple of hours even though they actually don't need it?

Mr Reed : That circumstance could occur. I definitely don't have any data at hand that says that is common. I don't think that is a common issue, but we can look at that and see what data we can provide.

Senator KOVACIC: Could you look at that and provide on notice whether you're seeing any patterns in relation to increases in daily hours.

Mr Reed : Yes. I'd have to see what data we have that could—let me take that on notice.

Senator KOVACIC: The worker retention payment—what was the take-up of that like? You mentioned, or someone mentioned—I think it was Mr Cook—that not all centres are on the worker retention payment. Do you have some data on the take-up of that?

Mr Reed : About 80 per cent of services signed up to the worker retention payment. That's about 205,000 educators that are covered by a worker retention payment grant. It's a pretty significant take-up, but it's not 100 per cent.

Senator KOVACIC: Is the department happy with the way the worker retention payment program is operating, and is there any intention to make any changes to that policy?

Mr Reed : I think it's fair to say that, when the worker retention payment was rolled out, there were some teething issues with the administration of the program that caused some backlogs and some delays for providers who applied in the initial stages. I am pleased to say that the backlog has been cleared, essentially, and new applications are being processed very quickly. There is still a need sometimes to request additional information from providers, but I think all the administrative issues have been resolved now and we are processing applications quickly. The feedback we get from the sector is overwhelmingly positive about the program and the impact that it has had on staff retention and ability to recruit staff. We're at record numbers of educators in the system now, with over 273,000 educators in the system, which is a pretty big growth over the last 12 months of over five per cent. I think we would say the worker retention payment is working well and working as expected. In relation to any changes to the program, that would be a decision of government.

Senator KOVACIC: I'm aware it would be a decision of government. I'm wondering whether, when you create a policy, there is advice as to how to make that better.

Mr Reed : Over the 12 months we have made some amendments to the policy. We've made a lot of administrative changes to the way we process and assess applications to make the external-facing interactions between government and providers much more efficient and effective. Changes have been made there. But there have also been some policy changes. For instance, we did some analysis of the services that hadn't signed up to the program and, going into the second year of the program, we altered the fee constraint policy. That enabled more services to sign up to the program. It captured some of those services that had exceeded the first-year fee constraint but not exceeded the two-year community fee constraint and allowed them into the program. That has been successful in getting more providers in. We have made some changes to the policy over the life of the program, but any significant future changes to the policy parameters would be a decision of government.

Senator KOVACIC: What percentage of workers does the program cover? Do you know?

Mr Reed : The one thing I would say is the number of educators covered by the program are estimates based on self-reporting from providers, so the program design doesn't necessarily require us to know exactly how many educators are being covered.

Senator KOVACIC: Really? So, you could have a centre register that could have 20 staff and only one is covered, and that would still be calculated?

Mr Reed : No. All educators are covered through the payment, but services self-report on the number of educators that are covered. The payment mechanism is designed on the charged hours of a service; it's not paid based on the number of educators. When the program was first designed, we estimated that approximately 200,000 educators would be eligible. Obviously, there's been some growth in educators since then, so it would be a little bit more, and we're currently at 209,000 potential educators covered. That's not quite all, but nearly all, educators, and we've exceeded our initial expectations for the number of educators that would be covered by the program.

Senator KOVACIC: To go back to my initial question, what percentage of workers is that?

Mr Reed : I'd have to probably—

Ms Crane : Without doing the calculations—we don't have the figure here—I could say that right now we have 209,342 that are already covered. There are another 960 who are on applications that are with the providers. They've applied and they're in the assessment process. So those two figures together are those that have applied for the worker retention payment, and the current employment numbers, as at the last time that they were taken, were around 273,800.

Mr Reed : Although not all of those would be eligible.

Ms Crane : Yes. We'll get to that in just a moment. The number is 273,800, and we know that obviously family day care and in-home care are not eligible at the moment. So we don't have a percentage to give you. But—just in terms of Mr Reed's comment that the vast majority are covered at the moment—between what we're seeing coverage of and those numbers and taking out the ones that are not eligible at the moment, there's a decent coverage.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you.

CHAIR: I'm going to Senator David Pocock and then Senator Hodgins-May.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thanks again for your time this afternoon. I'm interested if there's a policy position on the frequency of assessments at early learning centres and particularly—

Mr Cook : By state regulators? Is that—

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Yes—and whether or not centres should be reassessed following egregious or repeated breaches.

Mr Cook : It's a very good question. It's something that's got a lot of discussion happening at the moment across states and territories. As the regulator, Ms Crane's leading all those discussions, so I'll hand to her.

Ms Crane: There isn't a policy per se—going back to the start of the question. In August, at the Education Ministers Meeting, all states and territories agreed that they would do the assessment and ratings on average every three years, with a more frequent visit for those that are working towards. I can get the exact wording of that a little bit later. So that's the initial assessment and rating and obviously the reoccurrence of that over time.

In terms of the question about re-ratings, that can be done at any time requested by a service. Certainly, if they've failed on one of the standards or are working towards, they can go do that work and then ask for reassessment. Ministers have asked for a range of advice on other policy options. One of those does go to what happens when something has happened at a service and whether a rating should be suspended or otherwise altered. That's part of a live policy conversation with states and territories at the moment. But we'll come back to education ministers for advice.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Okay. Based on what you've seen, do state and territory regulators need more resourcing? At two ends of the spectrum, here in the ACT there's one centre that's had a number of breaches and has had no reassessment, and I was talking to an excellent not-for-profit who's been begging for a reassessment because I think it's been five years and they just want to be able to say, 'We're still exceeding expectations.' So is there a need for more resourcing? I think, from looking at the ACT data, they only did 54 assessments last year, which is 14 per cent of services.

Ms Crane : The decision on resourcing and how those resources are deployed is a matter for each state and territory. That's not something that the Commonwealth has involvement in. It's not something that we provide funding for. That is the responsibility of states and territories. So those decisions go to the ACT government.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. I understand fines for breaches of the national law have been tripled.

Ms Crane : That's correct.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: How many jurisdictions can actually levy fines?

Ms Crane : I would have to take that one on notice. I know there are a number of jurisdictions where I understand they may not have the required legislation or mechanism to recover. Others do. We'd have to go and gather that from the states and territories. We don't have visibility of that.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Here in the ACT, they can't actually impose fines, and they've said it would be very expensive to set up that system. What's the point of tripling fines at a federal level if, at a state and territory level, they have to not only do the inspections but also levy the fines, and they're saying, 'We can't actually levy fines'?

Ms Crane : A point of clarification—the law under which the state and territory regulators operate is not federal. It's called national law, but it actually isn't Commonwealth legislation. It is legislation that is passed by the Victorian parliament and then mirrored in other states and territories. The decision to increase was a decision by education ministers, who have oversight of that, and that change was then passed through. All ministers at that table need to have a consensus decision in order for that national law to be changed, which the ACT is part of.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Sure, but the federal government made a lot of the fact that they had tripled the fines. I'm sure most parents would be pretty shocked to read the fine print, and it says, 'Actually, you live in a jurisdiction where they can't fine.' They literally can't fine an early learning centre. How come jurisdictions actually having to sign up to be able to levy fines wasn't part of the discussions?

Mr Cook : That's more a question for the ACT minister. The ACT minister was part of the agreement to triple the fines. If there are mechanisms that she has to deal with in the ACT government, that would be something that she would have to work through. There's not much we can offer you on that because she was part of this decision-making process.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Can't this be something that's worked out through funding mechanisms? Obviously, the Commonwealth is on the hook for multiple billions of dollars.

Mr Cook : Sorry, which bit? That the ACT government needs to find a way to fine—

Senator DAVID POCOCK: No, for early learning.

Mr Cook : Sorry, you lost me.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: It's a federally funded—

Mr Cook : The childcare subsidy is.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: The Commonwealth is coughing up the subsidy. Surely, through that, there's a way to say: 'Listen, you've all got to be on the same page. We need to be able to levy fines.' No?

Senator Walsh: The national law is a law that is effectively owned by the Commonwealth and all the jurisdictions together. We come together as education ministers and make joint decisions. We made a joint decision to triple to penalties. I think Ms Crane has taken on notice trying to figure out what the situation in the ACT around that. When you describe them not being able to do that, that would not relate to the national law. It must relate to something about the ACT that we need to have a look at because it would be ACT specific.

There have been a couple of really significant changes on the front of Commonwealth childcare subsidy and the lever that it is. We do see that we need to be able to use the lever of the Commonwealth childcare subsidy to drive quality and safety in early education and care. We passed legislation last year to be able to withdraw Commonwealth childcare subsidy from providers on the basis of quality and safety. Interestingly, astonishingly, that wasn't the case before that legislation was passed. We are now using that legislation. We've put a number of services on notice—unless they improve their standards, we will withdraw their Commonwealth childcare subsidy.

In relation to seeking agreement with states and territories and how we're working together, these education ministers forums are a collective forum where we go and make decisions together. That's how it works on child safety and quality. In August last year, when the education ministers emerged from a big meeting on this, everyone was on a unity ticket about what needed to happen. There are many instances where something can get figured out in a jurisdiction, shared with other jurisdictions and then become the practice overall. That's effectively the way the system works.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I've been concerned watching what's happening at a federal level. I commend you, Minister, for a lot of the work that you're doing there. But because of this split between federal and state or territory, the state of play in the territory is that independent MLA Thomas Emerson put forward a motion to release a whole bunch of data relating to early learning, and this was opposed by the government, who said he was wasting time and there was nothing to see there. Finally, the motion went through, and they've had to comply with it. And we've seen some extraordinary breaches of faith and behaviour.

This is one sort of example to highlight why I'm asking these sorts of questions about the centre here, which changed management in August 2022. At the time, they were exceeding the NQS, including for staffing arrangements, but the government's website—the Starting Blocks website—shows that there have been five enforcement actions issued for this service in the last two years. It doesn't say what they were for. The documents that Thomas Emerson MLA got released for the last five years contained 49 documents for this centre, which includes serious complaints to the regulator, with reports of significant harm to children and compliance notices.

It is one of the centres with the most documents here in the ACT, and it includes a complaint from an educator at the centre in 2023, who'd been there for two years and said the centre was operating below their required educated child ratio almost every day, and staff were being denied morning and afternoon tea breaks. The doc also shows that the centre's nominated supervisor was barred from working in the sector in 2024 for conduct that was considered grossly negligent and likely to cause injury—repeated dislocations of a child's jaw because of limited to no supervision.

Yet the centre is still rated as exceeding the NQS. If you're a parent, you're trawling through these docs, you're seeing all this stuff, and then you go to the website and they're still exceeding that. That's not a system that's working. So how does the Commonwealth force the ACT government to actually get with the program here?

Senator Walsh: I'm happy to answer some of that. I think Ms Crane was going to jump in first.

Ms Crane : I was going to say that that exact scenario that you've just outlined is one of the reasons education ministers have asked us to have a look at what happens when a service has had those things happen. At the moment there isn't a relationship between that and the status of an assessment and rating. I think it's a very valid question and I'd ask the same thing as a parent myself. So then there are questions: What is it? Do we suspend it? Do we do another assessment and rating?

I think the transparency of this is not just through documents but also through the Starting Blocks website and is about trying to make sure that it is actually surfaced in the first instance. Then the other actions that education ministers have asked us to do go not just to transparency but also to making sure that that's accurate, that a parent can actually look at that and trust what they're seeing on it.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: So there's no way for the Commonwealth to say to states and territories: if you have a centre that changes hands, or if you have a centre that has a compliance notice against them, there has to be a reassessment within a certain period of time?

Ms Crane : All education ministers would have to agree to those processes or changes. There are obviously things at the moment that go to transfer of ownership and what happens with that, but if there were a change to that process under national law, all education ministers would need to agree to that. Now, the Commonwealth may propose something, but it does require all jurisdictions to actually agree to do that before anything can be passed.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Could you provide, maybe on notice, a bit more detail on the status of jurisdictions' ability to levy fines. I find it wild that jurisdictions that are effectively regulating an industry can't fine them under the law.

Mr Cook : I think that's only the ACT, to the best of my knowledge, but we'll take that on notice and come back to you on that.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you very much.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Following on from Senator Pocock's questioning, I've got some questions about obscene profits of for-profits. In 2024, a small group of large for-profit childcare providers made more than $122 million in post-tax profits—money that went to shareholders rather than being invested back into wages, conditions or service quality—such as G8, $67 million and Nest, $15 million. To put this into perspective, the total combined profit of this group of for-profit providers is greater than the top-up the government gave to support children with additional needs in the last budget, and it could pay for the consulting project that was outsourced to Deloitte more than 11 times over. At the same time, the government introduced the worker retention payment with a fee cap, recognising that public funding should come with conditions to ensure that it actually benefits workers and families. Does the minister agree that, when providers are making tens of millions of dollars in profit off the backs of our children, there is a clear case that public funding isn't being fully translated into better pay conditions and quality of care?

Senator Walsh: The way that we know that the worker retention payment is going into wages is because we've required providers, including those corporate providers, to enter into enforceable arrangements that effectively guarantee that the funding is going to wages. That can be through individual flexibility arrangements, or it can be through collective agreements. Eighty per cent of services have signed up. Many of them are services that are part of those corporate chains. Unless Mr Reed has anything to add to that, we are confident that the funding that we're providing is going into wages through the WRP. There were some other parts to your question about the cost.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I'm talking about the CCS in general, not just the worker retention payment. That was just one example. It's clear that the CCS is lining the pockets of for-profit providers and lining the pockets of their shareholders, rather than being reinvested back into quality and back into better conditions for our incredibly hardworking educators. I know you've said that you've worked with these educators. If you look at this and you look at that $122 million leaving the sector and going into the pockets of private shareholders, how does that make you feel? And do you think that that is reasonable and is something that parents, educators and families should reasonably expect to happen?

Senator Walsh: There's a lot in both of your questions there. I think I've dealt with the part on wages, unless you want me to go to wages again.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: No, it's more that taxpayer money, through the CCS, is being funnelled out.

Senator Walsh: What we're concerned about is that Commonwealth funding delivers quality early childhood education and that, whether a provider is for profit or not for profit, they put the safety and wellbeing of children first. We have made a number of changes to ensure that that is the case. One of them, which has been advocated for by many advocates for children, is to put safety and wellbeing as the paramount consideration in the law that governs the childcare subsidy. That has been part of allowing us to do what I was just describing to Senator Pocock, which is look at those providers who we may have concerns about around whether they are putting profit ahead of child safety and quality. If that's the case, we are now able to put those providers on notice and withdraw Commonwealth childcare subsidy. Just a couple of things on that—we are using those powers. We have put around 60 services on notice that they're at risk of losing their Commonwealth childcare subsidy. I think, more broadly, the kind of sector that we are driving through that and many other measures is a sector where, whether it's for profit or not for profit, in order to succeed, safety and quality have to be at the heart of everything they do.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I think that's the problem. We're just seeing headline after headline. I know that there's cracking down on individual cases, but, when you zoom out and you look at 122 million bucks leaving the sector, that's taxpayer money leaving the sector and heading offshore and heading into the pockets of people who don't give a rat's about our children's education. I know I come back every estimates and raise this, but it's leaving the sector. It's not going into improving the quality and the standards of our early childhood education and care system. I just don't know how any reasonable person or parent can look at that and say that's OK.

Senator Walsh: These are your feelings, and your assessment—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: No, it's not feelings. As someone who's worked as an educator, that feels that this is—

CHAIR: Could I ask that you don't talk over each other in these segments. It's very hard for me to monitor it as chair if I can't hear anything. Senator Walsh, if you want to provide an answer?

Senator Walsh: I'm not sure what the question is. It was a statement of your feelings about this. What was the question?

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Are you concerned about that scale of public money leaving the sector, not being invested back into improving quality conditions in our early learning system? Does that concern you?

Senator Walsh: I am concerned to be part of an early learning system, that is shared with the states and territories, that drives quality early childhood education for our nation's children, because quality early childhood education is a game changer for children. It's good for families, particularly mums returning to work, and it's good for the economy. We are driving safety and quality in everything that we do, and that includes the way in which we are approaching for-profit providers.

I am concerned to ensure that early childhood education is affordable for as many families as we can draw in to affordable early childhood education. That's why we did our cheaper childcare reforms that will save families $3½ thousand on what they would have otherwise paid. That's why we've capped fee growth in the sector, and, where we've capped it, it's now operating well below the long-term average. It's at around 3½ per cent. It's why we introduced the three-day guarantee of childcare subsidy for every child who needs it, irrespective of what their parents do. I am concerned for a quality early childhood education to be accessible to families in our outer suburbs, in our regions, and that is why we have implemented and are implementing the billion-dollar Building Early Education Fund, including announcing three of the first agreements with that fund to build services in places that need it.

We know that there's more to do on all of those things. The work on quality and safety will never end. We know that affordability is work that we need to keep doing. We know that ensuring that families have access to services where they live and work is a project that we'll continue to work on. We are putting safety and quality at the heart of our work. We have done that, literally, by making it the paramount consideration in the law that we are responsible for.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Thank you, Minister. I'm aware of that list of things. I'm trying to drill down into this particular issue. Beyond price caps, is the government considering stronger funding conditions, such as requiring excess or super profits to be reinvested into wages, staffing levels and quality improvements?

Senator Walsh: No.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Has any advice on this been prepared by the department?

That is also looking at the role of profits in that. That's the only thing I was going to add.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Evidence from The Hidden Lever report shows a link between improved pay and working conditions and better service quality and child outcomes. Given this, why wouldn't you be looking at ways to require the reinvestment of those super profits into improving pay and conditions?

Ms Crane : I think there's been coverage now a fair bit on the wages side of things. The worker retention payment is a response that is flowing back into the sector, and there is a requirement that all of that go to wages. We're seeing that in the evidence around the number of workers who are coming into this sector. They're staying in this sector. All of the indications are that that investment is working and it is working for attraction and retention for the workers that delivering these services.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: So, on that basis, I could safely assume that the department hasn't assessed how much of the $122 million in profits made by these providers could have been used to lift educator pay or improve conditions for the workforce if it were reinvested. That's not something that's been undertaken.

Ms Crane : Not in the way that you've just articulated. Mr Reed has covered off the service delivery price and its role in this.

Senator HODGINS-MAY:   I'm bringing forward questions from the sector, from parents who are really, I think, uncomfortable about continuing to subsidise a system where public money props up profits instead of improving pay and conditions. Senator Walsh: $3.6 billion is going to wages because we took that commitment to the election—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I look forward to hearing if that's continued.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Can you indicate whether you think safeguarding practices will be part of that.

Senator KOVACIC: Mr Cook, I just wanted to ask about the quarterly data tables published by the department regarding the childcare subsidy. Certainly what that's showing to us is, if anything, there are likely to be more places and they're seeing more demand than what we agreed with them last year. When I saw that data from the TACs, I was very surprised as well. It doesn't accord with what we're seeing directly from the universities.

Senator KOVACIC: Are you able to table that data for me?

Mr Turvey : It's not finalised at this stage. We're in the process of negotiating with the universities to get their evidence about what their demand is. So it's not really in a position where I can actually table it at this point.

Senator KOVACIC: When would you expect that data to be finalised?

Mr Turvey : Within the next few weeks.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. Well, once it's finalised, would you be able to table it then?

Mr Turvey : We can take that on notice.

Mr Cook : We can take on notice. That's fine.

Senator KOVACIC: Wonderful. Thank you. I guess my thinking is that we need a productivity boost to tackle the current challenges that we have with inflation and on the basis that a more highly skilled workforce generally leads to greater productivity. Are you concerned that we're currently managing the number of placements and offers based on the skilled workforce that we require? Have you done any modelling or other consideration of the implications if we don't have enough placements?

Mr Turvey : I'm not particularly concerned, given the demand that we're hearing about from the sector. There are a lot of things that you need to take into account in thinking about whether the supply in the sector is meeting demand for the economy in general, including the state of the economy and long-term trends. We are thinking hard about how the universities are meeting the needs of the economy and the skills needs, where skill shortages exist, but also the future trends. We're also looking very much at how the higher education system and the vocational education system work together. When you're thinking about demand and growth and how we meet skills needs, obviously, the higher education sector is part of that, but also the VET sector is a huge part of that. Potentially, up to half of the future skills demands will be met by the VET sector. We're looking at those issues. Obviously, the government set a target to achieve eight per cent of the population of post-school education by 2050. We're analysing what the trajectory of the education profile would need to look like to meet that.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. You haven't had any response or concern from the sector more broadly in terms of their inability or ability to meet the number of placements and the demand that they need?

Mr Turvey : The conversations we've been having or I've been having with the universities and with the tertiary admission centres suggests that the current round has been pretty orderly in terms of the process of making offers. Universities make offers; and they make second-round offers often. Universities are obviously trying to attract students. That process seems to be going well. I'm not seeing any evidence from the sector that people are concerned about that. We have some institutions saying they're seeing stronger demand; others are saying it's looking pretty much as they expected.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. And the data you were talking about before—are you able to talk us through a little bit of what you're seeing? I know once it's complete, you've taken that on notice, but can you just give us an indication of some of those trends of what you're seeing?

Mr Turvey : What we asked the institutions to give us was an estimate of their likely student load—new commencing student load in 2026. As I said, we had agreed with them a profile at the end of last year. Many of the institutions have come back and said, "Look, our demand profile looks pretty consistent with what we agreed at the end of last year", so they're not particularly concerned. A few institutions have come back saying that they're seeing stronger demand, but we're talking in the order of hundreds of places across a number of institutions. So it's not huge, but there are signs of strong demand.

Senator KOVACIC: When was that request made of the institutions?

Mr Turvey : I would need to check the precise details. I know we flagged with them before Christmas that we would be asking for that information. I think we might have formally asked for it early in the new year.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. And what is your expectation of when that might be provided?

Mr Turvey : That's trickling in now. We've got some of that information already. There are questions and follow-up that we're doing with the institutions. As I said, we expect—they're in the process of making offers now. They need some certainty.

Senator KOVACIC: Of course.

Mr Turvey : So we need to conclude that process in the next few weeks.

Senator KOVACIC: Sure. Then thinking about the comments you made about the admissions centre, can you share with me what evidentiary basis you have showing that significant decline of offers going through there, which is really concerning as a proportional figure if it's up to 50 per cent? Is it fully accounted for by the increase in the direct offers? Is it like one's down this much and the other's up that much?

Mr Turvey : Mechanically, that would be what you'd expect. I haven't drilled into the TAC data in detail. I have been talking to the TACs and scheduled to meet with ACTAC in the coming weeks to get a better handle on their data collection and the way—they don't all collect data in exactly the same way. Some of them may collect different things across the institutions. So we're working with them to get a better understanding of the data and that whole admissions process—how offers are made, when they're made and multiple rounds of offers. So that's one sort of information that we're examining with the TACs. Then, as I said, there's the separate engagement directly with institutions, which captures their non-TAC offer processes as well.

Senator KOVACIC: Sure. Has any work been done to confirm whether the estimates before Christmas that were provided to you actually match up with the actual decline shown by the TAC data?

Mr Turvey : We haven't cross-tabulated the two, Senator. I can't comment on that specifically.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay, thank you.

Mr Cook : Senator, just to help, just in terms of domestic load, the data that you've included includes postgraduate information, but, if you look at just those students who are beginning their university courses for the first time, based on the data that we've analysed from TAC, those offers are up by 2.5 per cent this year compared to last year.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay, thank you. So, as it stands, just to clarify, based on what you were hearing before Christmas, there was an estimate of offers. You were either on track or growing. We've seen a decline in the real terms in terms of the TAC data itself, but we can't cross-compare that because the non-TAC admissions we don't track. But you're comfortable that they're a significant proportion?

Mr Cook : I'm certainly comfortable with a significant proportion. Based on the conversations Mr Turvey has indicated, those direct offers have increased. Therefore, it's our view that the total pool of offers that have been made has increased this year compared to last year.

Senator KOVACIC: And the TAC data comes from January. The other data—is that historical?

Mr Turvey : The data that we've asked the institutions to provide is their estimates of current enrolments for 2026. So that's, real-time, their assessment of their likely demand.

Senator KOVACIC: Okay. Thank you, Chair.

CHAIR: Thank you. Senator Mulholland.

Senator MULHOLLAND: I'd like to ask some questions about the Commonwealth prac payment, which started on 1 July 2025 for eligible teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work students. Could you provide an update on implementation, and have all universities agreed to deliver the payment? Are any unis not delivering the payment? If so, could you take us through those unis and why they are not participating?

Ms Joldic : Sure. Early feedback from higher education providers has been really positive, and there's a high level of interest in applications of CPP from potentially eligible students. What the providers are reporting is that over 77,000 applications have been received in the first six months of the program and there is expected to be at least 68,000 domestic education students who will benefit from the program. This is the first time that the Australian government has provided financial assistance to support students undertaking mandatory placements. I will ask my colleague to provide further details in terms of how the program is rolling out.

Mr Nordstrom : I'm happy to respond to a few of the sub-elements of your questions there, Senator. In terms of overall numbers, as Ms Joldic has already mentioned, just under 78,000—I think it was 77,993 applications—were received within the first six months of the program. I think you asked how many universities are delivering the program, if I heard you correctly.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Yes, and if any aren't delivering.

Mr Nordstrom : All universities who are able to deliver the program are delivering the program. The nuance in my wording there is just that I don't believe the Australian National University has courses that are in scope. It's not that anybody has made a conscious decision not to deliver the program. In fact, it's probably appropriate to put on record the department's sincere appreciation for the support we have received from the sector to implement and deliver this program. We started with a bill—the Universities Accord (Student Support and Other Measures) Bill—that passed the parliament in November 2024 and received royal assent, I think, on 5 December that year. Then on 17 June 2025 the Minister for Education, following the authority that the Universities Accord (Student Support and Other Measures) Bill provided, inserted a new item—a new provision—into the Higher Education Support Act, a new purpose for which the government could issue grants to providers to support students for practicums. The Commonwealth payment program was then established by the minister on 17 June through amendments to the other grant guidelines, which formally established the program and the eligibility criteria that are in place. Then the payments to students were able to commence from 1 July. Block payments were given to providers to put them in a position to be able to issue funds to students. That has occurred from 1 July 2025. The only university that was not involved in that was the Australian National University—because of the nature of its core structures, not because of a decision not to be involved in the program.

I should say there was very strong collaboration and engagement with the sector between December 2024 and June 2025, when we worked through the details of the amendments to the other grants guidelines and also to establish what we call the Commonwealth payment program provider guidelines. That was done in deep consultation with the sector, and we were grateful for their assistance with that. They actually raised a number of issues to help us get that into a deliverable state for the sector.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Excellent. Of the almost 78,000 applications in the first six months, do you have a rough breakdown of how many applicants were in teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work? Have you got that data?

Mr Nordstrom : We won't have that as yet. The program receives structured reporting at the end of March and end of September each year. We have some high-level indications from providers about the numbers of applications but not yet the distribution of that across the fields of education. We won't have that just yet. But I should say for the record that, of those almost 78,000 applications that have been received, we know that already more than 71,508 of those have been processed by providers. Of those, 58,509 have been approved.

Senator MULHOLLAND: When you say 'processed', does that mean it's been approved or does it mean they've been paid—that they're receiving the payment?

Mr Nordstrom : For the 71,508 that have been processed, it means that the documentation has been received by the provider and can be assessed. Then the outcome of that assessment is the approvals, which is the 58,509.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Okay, great. Thank you. I'm going to shift gears to the study hubs. I'm not sure if I've got the right people up here. I do. Excellent—the dream team. Wonderful. I'm going to give a shout-out to the study hub at Strathpine in the seat of Dickson and the study hub in Moranbah in the seat of Capricornia. Both of those study hubs I've personally visited. One's obviously a regional or remote one and one is in an urban area. Both are fantastic. I was blown away by visiting them, so I'm going to ask a couple of questions just about the study hubs. Could you please take the committee through where that election commitment is up to. Our commitment was to double the number of university study hubs across the country, and I've seen lots and lots opening. I know the ministers have been really busy, as have our various members across the country, opening them up. Could you let me know where we're up to with that commitment to double the number of university study hubs in our first term?

Ms Joldic : I'll just provide a quick opening for this. The commitment has been exceeded, with the number of study hubs increasing from 34 to 71. Mr Nordstrom will take us through the detail of that.

Mr Nordstrom : In response to the Universities Accord, the government made the commitment to double the number of university study hubs. Further to Ms Joldic's point, since that time, a total of 35 additional study hubs have been established, 20 under the Regional University Study Hubs program and 15 under the Suburban University Study Hubs program, which we collectively call the study hubs. I'm pleased to be able to confirm that all of them are currently delivering services to students.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Excellent. There was even a chicken at the one I went to at Strathpine. There's a chicken as a pet for the students. It was an excellent place. My next question was going to be about the breakdown of the numbers, but you've already done that, so you've been ahead of me on that one. Now, I think you've probably covered the second question I was going to ask. I'm going to shift gears to another topic. There has been significant focus on improving university governance over the last 12 months. This includes the work from the Minister for Education, who is leading the state and territory education ministers and an inquiry by this same committee. Could you take us through where some of this work is up to and what are the next key steps?

Ms Joldic : Thank you, Senator. As you mentioned, there has been comprehensive work underway to lift governance standards at Australian universities to ensure that they meet expectations that students, staff and communities have demanded. This follows consideration by education ministers on a wide range of measures last year but also includes actually where the minister and government have gone beyond. On governance, generally, the Expert Council on University Governance principles are being written into the Commonwealth higher education regulation—the threshold standards. The principles provide clear guidance to strengthen governance and accountability in universities, drawing on best practice from the corporate and public sectors. There is an established process for changes to the threshold standards, and the minister has asked the Higher Education Standards Panel to consider and consult on proposed amendments. We expect consultation to happen in the coming weeks. The standards panel will also consult on additional transparency and reporting requirements which go beyond the expert council's principles and require universities to publicly disclose key information, such as consultancy spending. When that is enacted, universities will be required to report annually on compliance with these requirements on an if not, why not basis to TEQSA. There's also related work that is currently underway, which is the vice-chancellors' remuneration considerations of governing bodies and also consideration of skills matrices. The department has commenced work on that. I will throw to Ms Ryan to take you through the work that we're doing currently on vice chancellors' remuneration.

Ms Ryan : At the moment, the department is undertaking deep analytical work to understand how the vice-chancellors' remuneration framework could be structured and what that might look like. That involves things like considering institutional complexity. It involves things like comparative markets, what are notions of work value, proxies that might be used for those measures, whether or not there is sufficient data available to be able to have robust confidence in particular measures and, if there is not data available, what qualitative buttressing might suffice to supplement the framework. That work is underway. We are working closely with the Australian Public Service Commission and, through the APSC, the Commonwealth Remuneration Tribunal to help develop that framework. Just in relation to skills matrices as well, the department will be considering the ANU council's skills matrix, and that is with a view to understanding how representative that governing body is. Of course, it is ANU because ANU is the only national university established under Commonwealth legislation, but jurisdictions across Australia would also be considering the skills matrices of the governing bodies of universities established under their enabling acts as well.

Senator MULHOLLAND: Thank you. Lastly, how have you been finding the universities engaging with you in this work? Have you been finding that you've had good progress and good engagement?

Ms Joldic : From all of the discussions that we've been having, they've been very engaged in this piece of work. They see it as a priority piece of work. We haven't had any pushback that I'm aware of.

Senator MULHOLLAND: We love to hear that. Thank you. I'll hand back to you, Chair.

CHAIR: Thank you. Senator Faruqi, you have the call.

Senator FARUQI: Good afternoon, everyone. It's lovely to see you all. I have a number of lines of questioning in outcome 2. I might start with Job-ready Graduates. For how long will your government continue to bankrupt students through the Morrison government's cruel and punitive Job-ready Graduates scheme?

Senator Walsh: Thanks, Senator Faruqi. I might ask Mr Turvey or the department, after I've answered your question, just to go through some of the data that you've referred to there and check the data. Our focus in relation to that particular program is for ATEC to do the work to understand the real cost of teaching and learning, and Mr Turvey can speak to that work. The ATEC's job is to drive the long-term reform in the sector and for that to be based on really good evidence on what the costs of teaching and learning actually are. More broadly, we are focused on opening the doors to more university students in general. We have a target of 80 per cent of the workforce to have a tertiary qualification by 2050. It's only 60 per cent today. That is our focus with a whole range of programs and initiatives that we are rolling out, some of which have been spoken about already today, including the university study hubs; funding more university bridging courses; and, of course, rolling out paid prac as well, which is a great initiative to help people into degrees and staying in degrees. Senator FARUQI: Minister, just as a follow-up question, I think the data I have is pretty accurate. It's already been a few years since you've been in government. I do know that ATEC is going to look at just how much it costs, which could take a year. It has no—the way it is proposed at the moment in the legislation, it is not actually going to recommend to the government anything on student contributions, which could then take another year for the government to look into. That's at least two more years. Do you want arts students to suffer for two more years? Where is the urgency? I guess that's my question. Could I actually get an idea from the department about how long it is going to take to have any decision on JRG?

Senator Walsh: There's no doubt that there's a lot of work to do to rebuild our higher education sector after 10 years of cuts and neglect. Obviously, the first stage of that was the Universities Accord. We are really clear that is a blueprint that is going to take time to implement, certainly more than one term of government. We are implementing the recommendations of the Universities Accord, including—

Senator FARUQI: Minister, I'm sorry to interrupt, but it's not really urgent remediation. You could get rid of JRG today. There's a bill sitting in parliament for you to do that.

Senator Walsh: In terms of urgent remediation, of course, the concerns we had upon coming into government included a number of issues around HECS debt. We have focused on cutting HECS debt as a form of urgent remediation for students and recent graduates—$16 billion of student debt cut for more than three million Australians on top of fixing the indexing of that HECS debt in our previous term and fixing the thresholds at which people have to repay that debt. We're rolling out paid prac to teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work students as well because we want to help students with the cost of living as they are studying so that they can effectively complete their degrees and stay in those degrees that are so important. There's lots of work going on, Senator Faruqi. The accord was a blueprint to get us to that target of 80 per cent of the workforce having a tertiary qualification by 2050, and we are getting on with that job.

Senator FARUQI: Could I just get a quick response from the department as to your estimation on when JRG might be looked into and a decision made as to what's going to happen with that?

Mr Cook : That's a bit hard to answer because that'll be a matter for government. The work has begun around costing and pricing, and Mr Turvey can probably talk about that.

Senator FARUQI: When is that going to be completed—just a quick response?

Mr Turvey : We don't have a specific deadline to complete that work. I can talk you through the detailed mechanics of the work that we're doing. It's certainly underway. I would imagine later this year we would definitely have made progress. I'm happy to explain the details of what we're doing.

Senator FARUQI: No, that's all fine. I'm just looking at the urgency. There doesn't seem to be any urgency from the government. Senator FARUQI: It's not your role to comment on biases?

Mr Cook : You're asking me for an opinion—

Senator FARUQI: Minister, I ask you: are you concerned about these massive biases of this person who has been appointed to a role and that are going to impact these report cards?

Senator Walsh: The appointment of Professor Craven was a matter for Ms Segal. What we have done is establish the Antisemitism Education Taskforce, chaired by Mr Gonski. Senator FARUQI: Sorry, Minister, does Greg Craven have no liaison with that taskforce?

Senator Walsh: Sorry, Senator?

Senator FARUQI: Greg Craven—the person who has been appointed to lead the antisemitism assessments—what role does he play in liaising with the taskforce? Is there any consultation? How is it going to work?

Mr Cook : He attended the last taskforce meeting to provide an overview of the report.

Senator FARUQI: Yes, sure. So he's there. Minister, are you concerned about all these biases and how they're going to impact these assessments?

Senator Walsh: From a government perspective, we are concerned to ensure that universities are safe and inclusive places for students and for staff.

Senator FARUQI: The report card, among other things, will assess universities on whether they facilitate appropriate, rapid and effective responses to all protests, encampments and displays of flags, imagery and promotional material within university campuses and buildings. Senator FARUQI: The taskforce—isn't that responsible for the report card as well?

Mr Cook : No. The special envoy is responsible.

Senator FARUQI: It's not going to do any report cards or be involved in it. So the role of Greg Craven coming to the taskforce—what does that entail?

Mr Cook : It was to inform the taskforce of the work that he is doing with the special envoy. The reports have been developed by him. They'll go to the special envoy. They're not taskforce reports. It was an information session as opposed to the taskforce approving it.

Senator FARUQI: The Group of Eight Universities Chief Executive, Vicki Thomson, has called this report card assessment, all of that, a 'blunt instrument' to a much more complex problem. In response to the antisemitism envoy's plan, Universities Australia has said:

The danger of such a power being abused for political purposes is high and the chilling effect that such an approach would have on scholars and students is real.

Does the department have any concerns about the impact of all of this on academic freedom?

Mr Cook : Sorry—the impact of the report card?

Senator FARUQI: Yes—the antisemitism envoy's recommendations. This is what both GO8 and UA are concerned about.

Mr Cook : Universities Australia, as you know, are on the taskforce. I haven't had a direct conversation with UA around this, but the—

Senator FARUQI: Is the department still concerned about academic freedom?

Mr Cook : Concerned in the sense of—academic freedom is—

Senator FARUQI: In the sense of what the UA and GO8 had raised—blunt instrument, chilling effect on scholars and students, and many others have said similar things—because the way antisemitism might be assessed would be conflated with the criticism of Israel, for instance, as one example.

Mr Cook : Until the report cards are done, it's hard for me to say what that means for the sector more broadly. The report cards will be showing strengths and weakness, I would imagine, in relation to those things.

Senator FARUQI: You have seen the criteria, though, for the report cards, haven't you?

Mr Cook : Sorry?

Senator FARUQI: You have seen the criteria for the—

Mr Cook : Yes, I have got them. That's right.

Senator FARUQI: One of the recommendations of the antisemitism envoy is to increase antisemitism training in universities. Do you know if that has started?

Mr Cook : Additional funding was provided to Monash University to assist with that. It was $1.2 million, was it?

CHAIR: Senator Faruqi, if you've got more on this block, I'm happy for you to continue, but can I ask you please not to speak over the witnesses while they answer.

Senator FARUQI: I've finished on this line, so maybe—

CHAIR: I'll rotate the call and then I'll come back to you. Senator Kovacic, you have the call.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you very much. I want to ask some questions around the reporting about the CSIRO Industry PhD or IPhD candidate Mr Saryazdi—I believe I've pronounced that correctly—who has been charged with terrorism related offences related to a planned attack on Australia Day. In response, we have provided targeted support to members of our Jewish community, reinforced campus safety measures, increased security vigilance and ensure access to wellbeing and counselling services. The university reviewed its Socially Responsible Investment Policy in 2024 following wide community consultation, reaffirming our commitment to ethical and sustainable investment practices. When concerns were raised recently about the robustness of our investment approach, I immediately commissioned a further review to ensure our settings remain rigorous, transparent and aligned with community expectations. The findings will inform any necessary adjustments to maintain confidence in our governance and oversight.

As part of the response to the Nixon review into gender and culture, the university is establishing an office of integrity to strengthen reporting pathways, oversight and institutional learning. This office will provide a clear front door for staff and students seeking advice or support and will help ensure matters are handled fairly, respectfully and compassionately.

Financial stability remains a priority. Expenditure controls have helped stabilise the university's position; however, the operating environment remains challenging. Continued discipline must now be matched with a deliberate focus on rebuilding confidence, capability and long-term sustainability through revenue generation. Development of the next university strategy is underway through a co-design process involving staff, students, alumni, government and other stakeholders. This work is focused on clarifying institutional direction, strengthening governance and culture, and ensuring the university is well positioned for the years ahead. The new strategy will be launched in August this year, coinciding with our 80th anniversary.

Despite recent challenges, academic performance at the ANU remains incredibly strong. The university continues to perform at the highest levels nationally and internationally. We lead the sector with the highest retention and graduation rates of students from disadvantaged and underrepresented backgrounds, and we are home to one of the strongest Indigenous student communities in the country. We have listened carefully to our students, staff and the broader performance and music community about the importance of performance at the ANU School of Music. The university has established a new Performance+ Hub, which will provide the one-on-one tuition for students with strong performance ambitions.

At its core, the university is a community of students, scholars and staff united by education, discovery and service to the nation. Our focus now is clear and unwavering—advancing knowledge for Australia and the world and stewarding the nation's intellectual capital through our people, whose excellence underpins everything we do. Thank you, I welcome the committee's questions.

We are now in a situation where not only is it about the need to detect and respond to the use of AI in cheating but it's also about students feeling confident that the detection processes are fair and reasonable, that they get timely responses and that they are treated fairly in those academic conduct inquiries.

Senator KOVACIC: The figures also show that complaints about student services and the learning environment have also increased from 51 in 2022 to 232 last year. That's also a five-fold increase. Again, that's sort of consistent with all of the increases. So you can imagine, from just looking at them, people thinking, 'What's causing this phenomenon of all of these increases over time?' And I acknowledge that it's good that people are coming forward, but there's also that tipping point where you go, 'Hang on, this is a lot,' and, in many cases, it's four or five times. Do we have a big problem here?

Dr Russell : I would say two things. Once again, those matters are now being dealt with by the National Student Ombudsman and, I believe, their data says it is the highest, if not one of the highest, sources of complaints that are being dealt with by them—and, therefore, dealt with directly with universities. I would also say that it's been a real area of focus for us, particularly in our own liaison and consultation with students during and since the protests and encampments. We received intelligence at that time that students felt really unhappy about the accessibility and responsiveness, and they felt that the complaints and grievance services weren't student centred enough. We have issued a statement of regulatory expectation and very specific requirements for an uplift for student grievance and complaint services for providers. We consulted the developing ombudsman service at that time, and we certainly have had a lot of liaison back from universities about how they're needing to respond and do that uplift.

Senator KOVACIC: The safety data is another one that's flagged as a significant concern, both in relation to gender based violence and other wellbeing and safety complaints. In 2022, we had 16 complaints in two categories; last year, it was 76. They don't include, as you said, the data from the new Student Ombudsman. The data we have is that that was 1,711 complaints in the first six months. She's an external observer. It seems that safety on campus is really also deteriorating. Again, if you have any additional insights that are different to what you've indicated on the others—if there's something separately here that you're seeing?

Dr Russell : I think you'll find that, in part, the window that covers those increases in complaints covered a lot of the concerns that were raised with us by both Jewish students and students who felt vulnerable for a range of other reasons during the protests and encampments. It covered that window of time and their responses to those issues.

Senator KOVACIC: Was there definitely a link between those encampments and the uplift in complaints?

Dr Russell : Yes.

Senator KOVACIC: Is there a connecting thread or pressure point, such as inflation or the cost of living, that helps explain this consistent rise in complaints across the board? Are there any social elements that you're seeing that could be connected to that?

Dr Russell : We will go back and look at those data, but, certainly, from the preparation that we've done to be across that, there isn't another emerging theme. If there is, from time to time, we'll either focus on that in our compliance or we'll move ahead with some guidance or alerts to the sector.

Senator KOVACIC: So the only real social impact we've seen is the one relating to encampments and nothing else.

Dr Russell : In addition to gender based violence. But, of course, that is now dealt with by the regulatory function within the department.

Senator KOVACIC: My last question is: in all of those concerns in totality, noting your comments that it's good to see people come forward and have confidence to air grievances or complaints, what other steps is TEQSA taking to address concerns about the issues illuminated by the trends, generally speaking, of increasing complaints and what the problems on campuses are?

Dr Russell : I would say two things. One is that we, in consultation with students, which we do every year at our conference, are establishing a student advisory panel for TEQSA. One of the purposes of that is to understand, more directly and in more depth, the types of issues and concerns that students have on campus. That complements the regular engagement we already have with student peak bodies and the NTEU, on behalf of staff. We use those mechanisms, as well as our regular discussions with university administration, to understand those types of concerns. I think the student advisory panel is really, particularly important in that to make sure that we have that timely and meaningful connection with the things that are of concern and experience.

Senator KOVACIC: Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Faruqi, you have the call.

Senator FARUQI: The new proposed ATEC will likely have an impact on TEQSA. A lot of people and stakeholders who've submitted to the inquiry that is happening tomorrow have raised concerns about blurring stewardship and regulation when ATEC is set up. I'm just wondering, given that so many have raised these concerns, if there is a reason that TEQSA did not provide a submission to the Senate inquiry into the bill.

Dr Russell : We considered whether there were any key points in relation to the legislation specifically where we needed to make a submission. We felt that that was not necessary, obviously welcoming the fact that it's a matter for public consideration and consideration by the parliament.

Senator FARUQI: Sure. A number of stakeholders, in their submissions to the inquiry—and I'm repeating a bit of the question—are concerned about the potential for regulatory overlap and a lack of clarity of roles because that hasn't been really made clear in the legislation as far as I have seen it. Are you concerned about that? Obviously you still have to perform your functions. Are you clear, or do you think there are blurred lines?

Dr Russell : I might go to Professor Krause in the first instance.

Prof. Krause : Certainly we are clear about the fact that TEQSA has a very clear regulatory function using the Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021 as our guide. At the same time, we anticipate working closely with the ATEC and indeed we're already in discussion with the interim commissioners about appropriate governance arrangements and what would need to be put in place—firstly, to ensure that we do clarify where there might be potential for blurred boundaries and, secondly, to do all that we possibly can to reduce regulatory burden and sharing of data et cetera. Those are some of the steps we're already contemplating.

Senator FARUQI: Do you think that the role of ATEC in terms of being a strategic steward, not a regulator, needs to be further clarified?

Prof. Krause : It's a good question. I'm certain that, as the bill progresses, those issues will be part of the consultation and the finalising of the legislation. But, as your question alludes to, the need for clarity is important, and it's clear that that is something that is going to continue to be important as a new body is introduced into the sector.

Senator FARUQI: Concerns have also been raised with me about the Higher Education Standards Panel, HESP, being abolished. I guess there will be something in ATEC, not another panel. It's not clear what it will be. There is no protection of the independence and the expertise of this panel in the current bill as it stands. Has this issue been raised with you, and are you concerned about that?

Prof. Krause : I can certainly comment on the feedback that I've heard, and I have heard similar to what you've just mentioned. I think there are couple of things. First of all, I recognise that the bill is yet to be passed, so there's a consultation period in place. Secondly—

Senator FARUQI: You've said 'consultation' a few times. Who is the government consulting with now? Are you talking about the inquiry?

Prof. Krause : Tomorrow's inquiry for example, yes—and submissions have been sought. I'm certainly aware of the comments about the importance of having the function of setting standards. I think at this point it's really a matter for the process to take its course, and I certainly think the voices that have been heard about the importance of the independence of that standard-setting function have been loud and clear.

Senator FARUQI: Did the minister consult with TEQSA about any of the concerns that we're talking about today, about dissolving HESP and moving the functions into ATEC?

Prof. Krause : I'm not aware of specific consultation. TEQSA sits on the Higher Education Standards Panel with, I think, observer status officially. So, certainly, as part of the current Higher Education Standards Panel, we've been involved in discussions and we're aware of the draft legislation.

Senator FARUQI: Yes. In particular, about dissolving HESP, was TEQSA consulted by the minister?

Prof. Krause : I'm not aware of consultation specifically on that.

Senator FARUQI: It's a yes-or-no answer.

Dr Russell : With respect, it's not quite that simple. The minister seeks advice directly from TEQSA on a range of matters, but there's also an expectation that, as and when necessary, we contribute to advice from the department on related matters. So I would suggest that that is actually most properly a question for the department.

Senator FARUQI: Has TEQSA provided any advice to the department or the minister about abolishing HESP?

Dr Russell : We have had a range of discussions with the department at the ATEC. The role and function around the standards has been considered, because, obviously, the standards are critically important to us as a core regulatory tool. We have not provided any written advice in relation to that.

Senator FARUQI: I'm still surprised that you haven't provided a submission, because in our discussions you have agreed to quite a few concerns that I have raised, and you have also had discussions. So it's a bit of a surprise to me, but we might leave it at that.

CHAIR: Senator Pocock, you have the call.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Hello again, Dr Russell. Thank you for all the work that you continue to do, especially in regard to the ANU, and thanks for staying late. I acknowledge that you're often at the end of the night. I'm keen to ask some questions about the Briggs review and where things are up to. Last time you appeared, you gave an optimal timeline for delivery of the report from Ms Briggs in late February or early March. I'm wondering whether that's still on track or whether you could update the Senate.

Dr Russell : Ms Briggs is still preparing her report. It's not finalised yet. I know you've previously asked whether we would consider extra time for Ms Briggs were that required. Ms Briggs has made a request of me for some additional days to complete that report, and I have agreed and approved the costs associated with that. It remains most important to us that that report is right and thorough, so we're not interfering with that process. We're still hoping that it will be March. If it needs to run into early April, it will. I'm not at this stage expecting any extension beyond that time, but I will properly consider any request should that come.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: That's good to know. I understand that, from the timeline stated for TEQSA's decision on compliance, it was hoped to be delivered by April. This is for the ANU. Is that still on track, pending the completion of Ms Briggs report?

Dr Russell : It would depend absolutely on the delivery of the Briggs report. If I can, I will just explain the relationship between the two. We will, obviously, receive the report from Ms Briggs. Depending on the nature of the content, the findings and some of the particulars, we will need to afford to any individuals and the ANU, as an institution, procedural fairness around an opportunity to comment about any matters of fact or otherwise that they feel that they need to respond to. To do anything else would jeopardise a reasonable and fair outcome in the matter. So there will be whatever is required for that procedural fairness and response time. Then that will need to be considered by us before our compliance team finalise their assessment and make recommendation to our commission, because, of course, it's our commissioners who will make TEQSA's decision about whether there are any areas in which the ANU is falling short of the standards and any regulatory conditions or other regulatory action that is needed in response to that.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I have two follow-up questions on that. In terms of Ms Briggs report, has she provided interim findings? Does she relay things, or do you just get the final report and there it all is?

Dr Russell : She is still in the process of writing. We've had engagement with Ms Briggs about—we're absolutely scrupulous that there is no influence on her judgements or her findings. We have provided advice in relation to the extent to which she might need to refer directly to the standards, rather than form opinions in general terms—you know, those types of procedural and legal considerations in the finalisation of the report.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: If she has adverse findings against individuals in the ANU, what is a general timeline for that procedural fairness? Are we talking weeks? Months? How long does it usually take?

Dr Russell : I'll ask Mr Riordan to give an indication. I'm not sure there's a finite answer to that.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I understand, but—

Mr Riordan : As Dr Russell said, there's no specific timeframe. We really have to consider the nature of the findings, the factual matters and the amount of time that the ANU or individuals would reasonably require to respond.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Have there been any discussions with Ms Briggs and also within TEQSA about whether or not this report will be made public in part or in full? What's the usual process for that?

Dr Russell : That's not a matter for Ms Briggs. I have a position on that in principle, but we will need to consider it subject to the issues of privacy or vulnerability of any of those individuals concerned. My preference is that that report should be made public, but I would stress that I don't believe that should happen until after our commission have had a chance to consider that and arrive at their decision. Any public commentary, scrutiny or speculation around that report could potentially be perceived as biasing the commission, so I would see that as a step that would need to come after the commission have made their decision.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. Who would then make decisions around omissions, redactions and the potential publishing? Whose call is that?

Mr Riordan : I think our commissioners would have a view, and we would have a discussion.

Dr Russell : I suspect the buck would stop with me. However, we would take advice and consideration by the commissioners, and we would consider, obviously, legal and privacy perspectives as part of that. That's the best answer I can give you at the moment, Senator.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Fair enough. Whose decision is it to implement any recommendations that may be in the Briggs report—or Ms Briggs's report? In this instance, there are many Briggs reports. Is it the ANU's? The minister's? TEQSA's?

Dr Russell : You mean recommendations specific to ANU?

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Yes.

Dr Russell : The commission will consider any recommendations that Ms Briggs makes. In arriving at their own decision, they will consider whether they make findings, and they will consider, based on the requirements of necessity, risk and proportionality under our act, whether any regulatory action, particularly in the form of conditions, is imposed. Conditions carry an obligation of compliance on the institution. It's not the only tool in the toolkit. Matters can be agreed by undertaking, and in some cases that is appropriate and a timely way to deal with things. But it is really a question, ultimately, for the commission about what they feel is the necessary response.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I just have one or two more questions. I'm interested more in the process here. I don't want to make this into a hypothetical, but I'm just interested in how the TEQSA processes work. But this does sound like a hypothetical, so feel free to pull me up, Chair. In the event that there are adverse findings on whether individual members of council are fit and proper office holders, whose decision is to address those findings? Do you tell the ANU that they need to do something? How does that actually work?

Dr Russell : I can answer that. Would you prefer to answer that?

Mr Riordan : I'm in your hands.

Dr Russell : I may refer to Mr Riordan in a moment, particularly with respect to any other obligations the ANU has under its own legislation or the PGPA Act. There is a requirement, in relation to our act and obligations, that people in key leadership roles must meet the requirement for fit and proper persons. It is not necessarily the case that the Briggs report will make findings in relation to individuals that relate to fitness and propriety. You'll recall that the terms of reference are primarily focused on governance of the institution. She may or may not make observations that fall within that realm. However, we are very conscious that the investigation being undertaken by Dr Thom could also yield findings that may or may not go to fitness and propriety, so it will remain open to us, in terms of putting matters to the commission—if those findings are available in time, they might be dealt with as part of our current matter, but, should there be any findings even after the commission has considered the matters raised in the Briggs report that go to fitness and propriety, we would then consider putting those back to the commission. Would you like to correct me or add any other obligations?

Mr Riordan : Just a couple of things—one is that it is a condition of registration that both registered providers and personnel who make or participate in making decisions that affect the whole provider are fit and proper persons. I suppose, to the extent that a finding was being contemplated that that condition wasn't being met, as Dr Russell has explained, we would need to consider what, if any, procedural fairness would need to be afforded, and we'd also need to consider what, if any, action was to be taken about that condition if we considered that it wasn't being met. I'm really describing the agency's regulatory approach here, rather than dealing with a hypothetical scenario.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: That's what I'm interested in, so thank you very much. Again, thank you for all your work on this. Thank you, Chair.

CHAIR: That concludes our questions for TEQSA, which means it also concludes our hearing today. Thank you very much for appearing before us. I just remind all senators that the committee has agreed that any written questions on notice should be lodged with the secretariat by Thursday 19 February 2026. Thank you to Hansard, Broadcasting and our secretariat for all of their assistance.

Committee adjourned at 22:12
